catalog_quote: p.152, sec. 11 TONE TYPOLOGY: "Tone is a prominent feature of all Lakes Plain languages and therefore was most likely a feature of some of the protolanguages as well. This fact further distances Lakes Plain languages from the Trans New Guinea Phylum. All the modern languages have at least high and low tone. Duvle and Sikaritai have only these tones with Martin (1991) analysing the Sikaritai system as pitch-accent. The remainder of the languages also have combinations of high and low (or contours); Obokuitai has a fall (Jenison 1991), Doutai (McAllister 1991), Edopi (Kim 1995) and all the western Tariku languages have a fall and a rise (Clouse n.d.!)." p.160, Appendix 3: "Although tonal contrast is found in virtually all of the the Lakes Plain languages, it will not be shown in the word list transcriptions. Additionally, stress is not marked because only a few original word lists marked it and it has not been found to be contrastive in any of the Lakes Plain languages to date." p.164: "Language: Waritai / Elicitor(s): L. McAllister / Reliability: Obtained on survey. / Date: April 1986 / ... / Village: Taiyeve"

new_statements.rule_in_words: Family-level generalisation only: Lakes Plain languages (Waritai included by scope, as an East Tariku member whose data in this work is a 1986 survey wordlist) are tone languages with at least H and L; stress has not been found contrastive anywhere in the family, and no placement of (non-contrastive) stress is given for Waritai or for the family.
new_statements.exceptions: Hedges: tonal contrast in 'virtually all' Lakes Plain languages; stress non-contrastive 'to date'; only a few original wordlists marked stress at all. Sikaritai (sister East Tariku language) is noted as analysed as pitch accent by Martin 1991.
new_statements.domain_note: Not a description of Waritai prosody: the statement is a comparative surveyor's summary across the family, resting on published SIL phonologies of other members (Iau, Obokuitai, Doutai, Sikaritai, Edopi, Kirikiri). Waritai-specific material anywhere in print is limited to survey wordlists (McAllister 1986 in Clouse 1997; Voorhoeve 1975 no. 85 'Weretai') with tone and stress unmarked. Word-level (isolated wordlist items); no phrase-level information.
new_statements.first_reading: tone language with a stress statement
new_statements.identity_note: The quoted statement is about the Lakes Plain family as a whole (lake1255), not about Waritai specifically; Waritai (wari1264, = Voorhoeve's 'Weretai' no. 85, village Taiyeve) is covered only by scope. Do not confuse with 'Weirate', a Tause dialect also listed in Clouse 1997, or with the StressTyp Lakes Plain entry, which is Obokuitai (obok1239).

new_statements.quote: Unlike languages of the Trans-New-Guinea Phylum in the area, tone is a prominent feature of all Lakes Plains languages and therefore was most likely a feature of PLP as well. All the modern languages have at least high and low tone. Sikaritai has only these tones and Martin (1991) analyzes the system as pitch-accent. The remainer of the languages also have combinations of high and low (or contours); Obokuitai has a fall (Jenison 1991), Doutai (McAllister 1991), Edopi and all the western Tariku languages have a fall and a rise (Clouse n.d.), and Iau, because of deleting the segments of a syllable but not the tones, has more than one tone pattern on a syllable.

No sente…
new_statements.relation_note: Same family-level tone claim as the existing statement from Clouse 1997 p.152 (this 1993 paper is its precursor, nearly identical wording). It does NOT contain the 1997 App. 3 sentence that stress 'has not been found to be contrastive in any of the Lakes Plain languages' — the 1993 paper has no comparative wordlist appendix (App. 1 is the PLP vocabulary only), so it is silent on stress and adds nothing on placement. Compatible with the catalog's empty rule for Waritai.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Family-level statement only: every Lakes Plain language, Waritai included, is tonal with at least high and low tone; the article says nothing about word stress (the words 'stress' and 'accent' occur nowhere except 'pitch accent' for Sikaritai). Waritai itself appears only as an East Tariku member (tree p.27; population '?'), in sec. 6 pp. 13-14 (unusual initial consonant clusters shared with Sikaritai; a few cases of intervocalic flap deletion 'in Doutai and Waritai') and in the PET reconstruction *wari 'water' (p.20). No Waritai-specific tone pattern is given.
new_statements.exceptions: None on stress. Within the tone statement: Sikaritai has only H and L and is analysed as pitch accent by Martin (1991); the other languages add contour tones (Obokuitai a fall; Doutai, Edopi and all western Tariku languages a fall and a rise; Iau several patterns per syllable). Waritai is not singled out.
new_statements.identity_note: Clouse 1993 treats Waritai only as a member of the East Tariku family (tree p.27; sec. 6 pp. 13-14 segmental remarks; PET *wari 'water' p.20); the tone statement is about all Lakes Plain languages collectively, not Waritai in particular. No dialect is named. Waritai data in both Clouse papers derive from the same 1986 survey wordlist (L. McAllister, Taiyeve), so this is not an independent description.
